country.comment: The study focuses empirically on rural counties in Guizhou Province in southwest China within the national Rural Drinking Water Safety Project.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF pp. 7–8, Section 'RESEARCH DESIGN'

effect_estimate.comment: Main dependent variables are cumulative 2010–2013 county-level beneficiaries and MWR project funds (reported in 10,000 RMB units in Tables 1, 3, A2, A3, and A5). Direct post-construction household drinking water access was not tracked by MWR records.
effect_estimate.value: Counties with larger ethnic-minority population shares received significantly less government drinking water infrastructure support (2010–2013 cumulative MWR projects, N = 61 counties, OLS with robust SEs): Percentage Minority was negatively associated with project beneficiaries in Model 1 (b = –83,928.93, SE = 26,889.73, p < 0.01, R² = 0.5441) and full Model 2 controlling for county autonomy and leader ethnicity (b = –75,817.29, SE = 36,428.49, p < 0.05, R² = 0.5655), as well as project funding (b = –3,764.79, SE = 1,853.63, p < 0.05, Model 6, Table A3) and prefecture-nested multilevel models (beneficiaries b = –70,883.79, SE = 34,318.85, p < 0.05; funds b = –3,136.75, SE = 1,682.30, p < 0.05, Table A5). Predicted beneficiaries declined from 143,687.2 (funds: RMB 7,069.40) in counties with <18% minority share to 96,448.77 (funds: RMB 4,624.92) in counties with >80% minority share (Table 3). Formal minority autonomous county status significantly reversed the negative slope in interaction Model 3 (Percentage Minority b = –89,692.21, SE = 33,573.31, p < 0.05; Autonomous County b = –236,074.3, SE = 97,292.2, p < 0.05; Minority × Autonomous b = 283,665, SE = 134,640.5, p < 0.05, Table 4), whereas county leader ethnicity had no significant main or interactive effect (Minority × Share Han Leader b = 105,291.60, SE = 105,700.20, Model 4, Table 4).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 15, Table 2; PDF p. 16, Table 3 & text; PDF p. 17, Table 4; PDF p. 26, Table A3; PDF p. 27, Table A5

mechanism_certainty.comment: Cross-sectional observational design (ceiling <= 2). Coded 1 (documented association) because the primary empirical analysis establishes county-level statistical associations between ethnic share, formal minority autonomous county status, leader ethnicity, and MWR project beneficiaries/funding without directly measuring bureaucratic discretion in the dataset or tracking post-project household water access outcomes (PDF pp. 10, 20), supplemented only by brief illustrative fieldwork anecdotes.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 9–10, Section 'Variables and Measurement'; PDF pp. 14–19, Section 'RESULTS'; PDF p. 20, Section 'CONCLUSION'

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines decentralized local bureaucrats' implementation discretion in project allocation under short cadre-evaluation timelines (discretion), formal minority autonomous county/prefecture institutional status and preferential policy (accommodation), vertical central-provincial-county fiscal/political relationships and co-ethnic county Party/government leadership (political_coordination), and officials' avoidance of village/community input to speed project completion (participation).
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 2–7, Sections 'IMPLEMENTATION MATTERS' & 'Minority Autonomy and Co-ethnic Leaders'; PDF pp. 11–13, Sections 'Autonomy' & 'Co-ethnic Leaders'

outcome_flags.comment: Measures the cumulative number and county population share of intended beneficiaries covered by new government-funded rural safe drinking water infrastructure projects (service_coverage) aimed at expanding rural safe drinking water provision (water_access), though post-construction household access was not directly verified (PDF pp. 10, 20).
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 8–10, Sections 'RESEARCH DESIGN' & 'Variables and Measurement'; PDF p. 15, Table 2

publication_year.comment: Published in Asian Survey, Vol. 60, No. 4 (2020).
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, journal footer and DOI line

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary empirical design is a quantitative observational cross-sectional county-level regression analysis (aggregating 2010–2013 project totals to a single county cross-section regressed on 2010 census and administrative covariates without a quasi-experimental intervention comparator). Although the author mentions corroborative field visits to >50 villages and interviews, there is no qualitative methods protocol or qualitative results section warranting MMAT.
risk_of_bias_tool.value: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF pp. 7–15, Sections 'RESEARCH DESIGN' & 'RESULTS'; PDF p. 15, Table 2; PDF p. 27, Table A5

sample_size.comment: Total province universe is 82 counties across 9 prefectures in Guizhou (Table A2); multivariable OLS and multilevel regression models analyze N = 61 counties (nested in 9 prefectures in Table A5) due to missing village-count and karst-topography covariates (PDF p. 16). Exact number of qualitative interviews is not reported.
sample_size.value: 82 counties in Guizhou Province (regression analytic sample N = 61 counties nested in 9 prefectures), aggregating 13,376 Ministry of Water Resources drinking water projects (2010–2013) and 360 county officials (186 Party secretaries and 174 governors); corroborated by visits to over 50 villages and interviews
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 8, Section 'RESEARCH DESIGN'; PDF pp. 9–12, Section 'Variables and Measurement'; PDF p. 15, Table 2; PDF p. 25, Table A2; PDF p. 27, Table A5

study_design.comment: Cumulative 2010–2013 MWR project records are aggregated into a single county-level cross-section and analyzed against 2010 census, leadership, and geographic variables via OLS and two-level prefecture/county random-effects models.
study_design.value: Observational cross-sectional county-level quantitative analysis (multivariable OLS regressions with robust standard errors and multilevel random-effects models of cumulative 2010–2013 drinking water infrastructure beneficiaries and funding), corroborated by field visits and qualitative interviews
study_design.where_found: PDF pp. 7–14, Section 'RESEARCH DESIGN'; PDF pp. 14–19, Section 'RESULTS'; PDF p. 27, Table A5
